name: AceDB
tagline: Genome database system born for C. elegans in 1989, with an object-tree data model; NCBI fork still updated.
description: AceDB (A C. elegans DataBase) is a genome database and browser that Richard Durbin and Jean Thierry-Mieg started around 1989-1990 for the nematode C. elegans, later reused for many other organisms and as the original core of WormBase. Data lives in classes of objects whose schema is a tree of tagged fields, which made it flexible for fast-changing biological knowledge long before document databases; it ships its own query language (AQL), table maker and graphical browsers. In the late 1990s the code forked: the Sanger Institute branch was archived on GitHub in October 2016, while Jean Thierry-Mieg's NCBI branch, used for AceView and RNA-seq tooling, still receives source updates (latest tarball May 2025). It is a niche tool for groups with existing AceDB data, not a general-purpose database.
statusNote: Sanger branch archived in 2016; the NCBI fork maintained by Jean Thierry-Mieg still publishes source updates (May 2025) but has a tiny user base.
developer: Richard Durbin and Jean Thierry-Mieg (NCBI / Sanger Institute)

scale.notes: Single-server database files; used for whole-genome annotation datasets of its era.

strengths: Tree-structured object schema absorbs evolving biological annotations without migrations
Integrated graphical genome browsers and table maker for biologists
Decades of curated genomic datasets (WormBase, AceView) were built on it
GPL source still available from both the Sanger and NCBI branches
weaknesses: Tiny, ageing user and developer community
Two diverged forks with uneven documentation
Non-standard query language and file formats with little tooling outside bioinformatics
No replication, clustering or modern security features
useCases: Maintaining legacy AceDB/WormBase-era genome annotation datasets
Working with NCBI AceView and Magic RNA-seq pipelines
notIdealFor: New bioinformatics platforms (prefer PostgreSQL-based schemas or genomics stores)
